name: Eye color change surgery (keratopigmentation / iris implants)

lead: Two kinds of procedure aim to change the apparent colour of healthy eyes: cosmetic iris implants, such as NewColorIris and BrightOcular, which are silicone discs placed in front of the natural iris, and keratopigmentation, which tints the cornea. The payoff people want is a different eye colour, visible as soon as the procedure is done.

Implants cover the natural iris with a coloured disc, while keratopigmentation deposits pigment in corneal layers, with femtosecond lasers used in newer versions. Published literature on cosmetic iris implants is largely case reports and case series. A 2023 review states that iris implants were designed for conditions such as aniridia and are not approved by regulators anywhere for cosmetic use in healthy eyes.

paras: Both are eye surgeries done by ophthalmic surgeons, often abroad, with the colour change visible once the eye heals. Some people consider coloured contact lenses as a non-surgical alternative.

Reported problems include corneal decompensation or damage, raised eye pressure and glaucoma, inflammation and vision loss. Cosmetic iris implants are not approved by regulators anywhere, and vision-threatening complications are the main finding in the literature.

angle.text: An implant or corneal pigment changes the apparent colour of the iris, so the colour shift is visible once the procedure is done. Published reports mainly document complications, and cosmetic iris implants are not approved by regulators.

lead: Eye color change surgery refers to procedures intended to alter the apparent color of healthy eyes. Two approaches are discussed: cosmetic iris implants, such as NewColorIris and BrightOcular, which are placed inside the eye in front of the natural iris, and keratopigmentation, in which pigment is deposited in the cornea [1].

Published literature on cosmetic iris implants consists largely of case reports and case series describing complications including corneal decompensation, raised eye pressure, inflammation and vision loss [2]. A 2023 review states that iris implants were designed for conditions such as aniridia and are not approved by regulators anywhere for cosmetic use in healthy eyes.
infobox: Iris implants not approved for cosmetic use anywhere, per a 2023 review
BrightOcular described as removable [1]; keratopigmentation difficult to control [1]

paras: Iris implants were first described for treating photophobia and glare from aniridia, coloboma and other iris defects; the same devices have been used cosmetically in healthy eyes. The earlier NewColorIris implant is reported to have a record of high ocular morbidity and is no longer in use, while a newer BrightOcular design added grooves intended to lessen iris contact and permit fluid flow [2].

Corneal tattooing, or keratopigmentation, has been used for centuries to mask corneal scars; Wikipedia traces it to Galen in the second century and notes that femtosecond-laser methods (FLAAK) are now used on healthy eyes to change color and have become popular on social media [1]. Reported complications of corneal tattooing in general include redness, keratitis, ulceration and fading or unpredictable results [1].

A 2016 case series of patients who had BrightOcular implants placed solely for cosmetic reasons reported iritis, glaucoma and corneal decompensation [2], and a 2015 JAMA Ophthalmology report linked a newer cosmetic implant to corneal endothelial cell loss and iritis [3]. Case reports describe progressive corneal edema and glaucoma needing trabeculectomy and implant removal, and complications emerging 15 years after an uneventful procedure. The 2023 review attributes harms to mechanical irritation of angle structures, chronic inflammation, pigment dispersion and endothelial cell loss.
No controlled trials of cosmetic iris implants or keratopigmentation for eye color change were found. Evidence consists of case reports and case series [2][3].
